claim: Anillin is a scaffolding protein that was first characterized for its role in cell division.
source: Anillin is a scaffolding protein that was first characterized for its role in cell division (Field and Alberts, 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Field and Alberts, 1995.

claim: Anillin regulates cytokinesis in organisms ranging from yeast to humans.
source: has since been shown to regulate cytokinesis in organisms ranging from yeast to humans (Piekny and Maddox, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Piekny and Maddox, 2010.

claim: Anillin localizes to the actomyosin contractile ring during cytokinesis.
source: Anillin localizes to the actomyosin contractile ring during cytokinesis and primarily to the nucleus during interphase (Field and Alberts, 1995; Oegema et al., 2000; D'Avino, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Field and Alberts, 1995; Oegema et al., 2000; D'Avino, 2009.

claim: Anillin localizes primarily to the nucleus during interphase.
source: Anillin localizes to the actomyosin contractile ring during cytokinesis and primarily to the nucleus during interphase (Field and Alberts, 1995; Oegema et al., 2000; D'Avino, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Field and Alberts, 1995; Oegema et al., 2000; D'Avino, 2009.

claim: During cytokinesis, anillin anchors the contractile ring to the plasma membrane by binding to actomyosin through its N-terminal myosin- and F-actin-binding domains.
source: During cytokinesis, anillin anchors the contractile ring to the plasma membrane by binding to actomyosin through its N-terminal myosin- and F-actin-binding domains and to lipids through its C-terminal C2 and PH domains (Straight et al., 2005; Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Straight et al., 2005; Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2015.

claim: During cytokinesis, anillin anchors the contractile ring to the plasma membrane by binding to lipids through its C-terminal C2 and PH domains.
source: During cytokinesis, anillin anchors the contractile ring to the plasma membrane by binding to actomyosin through its N-terminal myosin- and F-actin-binding domains and to lipids through its C-terminal C2 and PH domains (Straight et al., 2005; Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Straight et al., 2005; Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Anillin can both enhance and limit contractility during cytokinesis through binding directly to active RhoA.
source: Anillin can both enhance and limit contractility during cytokinesis through binding directly to active RhoA as well as several proteins that positively or negatively regulate Rho, and by crosslinking F-actin (Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Frenette et al., 2012; Manukyan et al., 2015; Descovich et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Frenette et al., 2012; Manukyan et al., 2015; Descovich et al., 2018.

claim: Anillin can both enhance and limit contractility during cytokinesis by binding to several proteins that positively or negatively regulate Rho.
source: Anillin can both enhance and limit contractility during cytokinesis through binding directly to active RhoA as well as several proteins that positively or negatively regulate Rho, and by crosslinking F-actin (Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Frenette et al., 2012; Manukyan et al., 2015; Descovich et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Frenette et al., 2012; Manukyan et al., 2015; Descovich et al., 2018.

claim: Anillin can both enhance and limit contractility during cytokinesis by crosslinking F-actin.
source: Anillin can both enhance and limit contractility during cytokinesis through binding directly to active RhoA as well as several proteins that positively or negatively regulate Rho, and by crosslinking F-actin (Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Frenette et al., 2012; Manukyan et al., 2015; Descovich et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Piekny and Glotzer, 2008; Frenette et al., 2012; Manukyan et al., 2015; Descovich et al., 2018.

claim: Anillin is localized to cell–cell junctions in frog embryos.
source: Our group showed that anillin is localized to cell–cell junctions in frog embryos where it regulates cell–cell junction integrity, as both tight junctions and adherens junctions were disrupted when anillin was knocked down (Reyes et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reyes et al., 2014.

claim: Anillin regulates cell–cell junction integrity in frog embryos, as both tight junctions and adherens junctions were disrupted when anillin was knocked down.
source: Our group showed that anillin is localized to cell–cell junctions in frog embryos where it regulates cell–cell junction integrity, as both tight junctions and adherens junctions were disrupted when anillin was knocked down (Reyes et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reyes et al., 2014.

claim: Anillin scaffolds the contractile actomyosin machinery connected to epithelial cell–cell junctions.
source: Furthermore, we showed that anillin scaffolds the contractile actomyosin machinery connected to epithelial cell–cell junctions (Reyes et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reyes et al., 2014.

claim: Proteomic studies supported anillin's association with cadherin-mediated adhesions in fly and human cells.
source: Proteomic studies supported anillin's association with cadherin-mediated adhesions in fly and human cells (Guo et al., 2014b; Toret et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2014b; Toret et al., 2014.

claim: Anillin knockdown in cultured human epithelial cells resulted in junction disassembly and disorganized junctional F-actin and myosin II.
source: Anillin knockdown in cultured human epithelial cells resulted in junction disassembly and disorganized junctional F-actin and myosin II (Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Myosin II anchors anillin to the apical cell cortex.
source: A recent study reported that myosin II anchors anillin to the apical cell cortex, and cycles of binding and unbinding to anillin stabilize active RhoA by increasing its cortical residence time, thus promoting junctional actomyosin contractility (Budnar et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Budnar et al., 2018.

claim: Cycles of binding and unbinding of myosin II to anillin stabilize active RhoA by increasing its cortical residence time, thus promoting junctional actomyosin contractility.
source: A recent study reported that myosin II anchors anillin to the apical cell cortex, and cycles of binding and unbinding to anillin stabilize active RhoA by increasing its cortical residence time, thus promoting junctional actomyosin contractility (Budnar et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Budnar et al., 2018.

claim: Barrier function in the kidney, which is mediated by tight junctions, was compromised by a mutation in anillin that causes Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis.
source: Finally, in vivo studies in zebrafish demonstrated that barrier function in the kidney, which is mediated by tight junctions, was compromised by a mutation in anillin that causes Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis, a leading cause of kidney failure (Gbadegesin et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gbadegesin et al., 2014.

claim: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis is a leading cause of kidney failure.
source: Finally, in vivo studies in zebrafish demonstrated that barrier function in the kidney, which is mediated by tight junctions, was compromised by a mutation in anillin that causes Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis, a leading cause of kidney failure (Gbadegesin et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gbadegesin et al., 2014.

claim: Anillin is expressed during developmental events that are controlled by mechanical inputs from cells and tissues, including gastrulation and neurulation.
source: Notably, anillin is expressed during developmental events that are controlled by mechanical inputs from cells and tissues, including gastrulation and neurulation (Session et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Session et al., 2016.

claim: Anillin is overexpressed in multiple human cancers.
source: Anillin is also overexpressed in multiple human cancers (Hall et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2005.

claim: Increased tissue stiffness is frequently observed during tumorigenesis.
source: Increased tissue stiffness is frequently observed during tumorigenesis; tumor growth and metastases are sensitive to mechanical cues, which can significantly affect cancer prognosis (Kumar and Weaver, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kumar and Weaver, 2009.

claim: Tumor growth and metastases are sensitive to mechanical cues, which can significantly affect cancer prognosis.
source: Increased tissue stiffness is frequently observed during tumorigenesis; tumor growth and metastases are sensitive to mechanical cues, which can significantly affect cancer prognosis (Kumar and Weaver, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kumar and Weaver, 2009.

claim: Changes in mechanical properties can be mediated by changes in the composition of the extracellular matrix.
source: Changes in mechanical properties can be mediated by changes in the composition of the extracellular matrix as well as changes in the organization of the intracellular cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a general statement about mechanical properties based on established knowledge.

claim: Changes in mechanical properties can be mediated by changes in the organization of the intracellular cytoskeleton.
source: Changes in mechanical properties can be mediated by changes in the composition of the extracellular matrix as well as changes in the organization of the intracellular cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a general statement about mechanical properties based on established knowledge.

claim: Anillin resides not only in the nucleus of interphase cancer cells, but also in the cytoplasm.
source: Anillin resides not only in the nucleus of interphase cancer cells, but also in the cytoplasm, and anillin expression can have either positive or negative outcomes for patients depending on the cancer type and anillin's subcellular localization (Hall et al., 2005; Suzuki et al., 2005; Ronkainen et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2015; Magnusson et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Idichi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2005; Suzuki et al., 2005; Ronkainen et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2015; Magnusson et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Idichi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Anillin expression can have either positive or negative outcomes for patients depending on the cancer type and anillin's subcellular localization.
source: Anillin resides not only in the nucleus of interphase cancer cells, but also in the cytoplasm, and anillin expression can have either positive or negative outcomes for patients depending on the cancer type and anillin's subcellular localization (Hall et al., 2005; Suzuki et al., 2005; Ronkainen et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2015; Magnusson et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Idichi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2005; Suzuki et al., 2005; Ronkainen et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2015; Magnusson et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Idichi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: High junctional tension induces a conformational change in α-catenin, which recruits vinculin to adherens junctions to reinforce the connection to the actin cytoskeleton.
source: High junctional tension induces a conformational change in α-catenin, which recruits vinculin to adherens junctions to reinforce the connection to the actin cytoskeleton (Yonemura et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yonemura et al., 2010.

claim: Tricellular contacts are sites of higher tension.
source: In control embryos, Vinculin-mNeon accumulated weakly along bicellular junctions and strongly at tricellular contacts, which are sites of higher tension (Figure 1A) (Choi et al., 2016; Higashi and Miller, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2016; Higashi and Miller, 2017.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, the intensity of Vinculin-mNeon was reduced at junctions.
source: When anillin was knocked down, the intensity of Vinculin-mNeon was reduced at junctions (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, mCherry-α-catenin was strongly reduced at junctions.
source: When anillin was knocked down, mCherry-α-catenin was strongly reduced at junctions; therefore, the reduced Vinculin-mNeon intensity may not indicate reduced tension because α-catenin is also reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: When anillin was overexpressed, the intensity of Vinculin-mNeon at junctions was significantly elevated.
source: Notably, when anillin was overexpressed, the intensity of Vinculin-mNeon at junctions was significantly elevated (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: When anillin was overexpressed, the intensity of mCherry-α-catenin was unchanged.
source: when anillin was overexpressed, the intensity of Vinculin-mNeon at junctions was significantly elevated (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), and the intensity of mCherry-α-catenin was unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: The increased Vinculin-mNeon recruitment when anillin was overexpressed was due to a tension-induced conformation change in α-catenin.
source: when anillin was overexpressed, the intensity of Vinculin-mNeon at junctions was significantly elevated (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), and the intensity of mCherry-α-catenin was unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C), indicating that the increased Vinculin-mNeon recruitment was due to a tension-induced conformation change in α-catenin
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing increased vinculin without increased α-catenin.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, cells became less polygonal and more rounded.
source: When anillin was knocked down, cells became less polygonal and more rounded (Figure 1A), a hallmark of reduced tension (Yonemura et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Yonemura et al., 2010.

claim: Cell rounding is a hallmark of reduced tension.
source: When anillin was knocked down, cells became less polygonal and more rounded (Figure 1A), a hallmark of reduced tension (Yonemura et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yonemura et al., 2010.

claim: When anillin was overexpressed, junctions exhibited a wavy, distorted shape compared to more linear control junctions.
source: In contrast, when anillin was overexpressed, junctions exhibited a wavy, distorted shape compared to more linear control junctions (Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wavy junctions can indicate unbalanced high tension.
source: Interestingly, wavy junctions can indicate either unbalanced high tension (Tokuda et al., 2014; Nowotarski and Peifer, 2014) or uniform low tension along the junction (Nowotarski and Peifer, 2014; Choi et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tokuda et al., 2014; Nowotarski and Peifer, 2014.

claim: Wavy junctions can indicate uniform low tension along the junction.
source: Interestingly, wavy junctions can indicate either unbalanced high tension (Tokuda et al., 2014; Nowotarski and Peifer, 2014) or uniform low tension along the junction (Nowotarski and Peifer, 2014; Choi et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nowotarski and Peifer, 2014; Choi et al., 2016.

claim: The amount of junction recoil is reported to correlate with the relative junctional tension such that a junction under high tension will exhibit enhanced recoil.
source: The amount of junction recoil (measured as the distance between cell vertices over time) is reported to correlate with the relative junctional tension such that a junction under high tension will exhibit enhanced recoil (Farhadifar et al., 2007; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Farhadifar et al., 2007; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009.

claim: After laser ablation, control junctions recoiled 2.8 ± 0.2 µm after 18 s.
source: After laser ablation, control junctions recoiled 2.8 ± 0.2 µm after 18 s (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Video 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Video 1.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, junction recoil increased to 4.1 ± 0.4 µm after 18 s.
source: Based on our hypothesis that anillin promotes junctional tension, we expected to see reduced junction recoil when anillin was knocked down; however, recoil increased to 4.1 ± 0.4 µm after 18 s (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Video 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Video 1.

claim: When anillin was overexpressed, junction recoil decreased to 1.6 ± 0.4 µm after 18 s.
source: When anillin was overexpressed, we expected to see increased recoil; however, the recoil decreased to 1.6 ± 0.4 µm after 18 s (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Video 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Video 1.

claim: After 45 s, control cells and anillin knock down cells reached a similar amount of recoil.
source: After 45 s (the last time point where we could accurately track the junction vertices), control cells and anillin knock down cells reached a similar amount of recoil, while anillin overexpressing cells recoiled significantly less than controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: After 45 s, anillin overexpressing cells recoiled significantly less than controls.
source: After 45 s (the last time point where we could accurately track the junction vertices), control cells and anillin knock down cells reached a similar amount of recoil, while anillin overexpressing cells recoiled significantly less than controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Anillin overexpressing cells separate perpendicularly slightly, but not significantly, more often than control cells.
source: Using E-cadherin 'splaying' (meaning that the stubs of the junction left after laser ablation were separated in two) as a readout of perpendicular separation, we found that anillin overexpressing cells separate perpendicularly slightly, but not significantly, more often than control cells, whereas perpendicular separation of anillin knockdown cells is dramatically reduced compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Perpendicular separation of anillin knockdown cells is dramatically reduced compared to controls.
source: Using E-cadherin 'splaying' (meaning that the stubs of the junction left after laser ablation were separated in two) as a readout of perpendicular separation, we found that anillin overexpressing cells separate perpendicularly slightly, but not significantly, more often than control cells, whereas perpendicular separation of anillin knockdown cells is dramatically reduced compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Knocking down anillin reduced the intensity of the medial-apical F-actin network.
source: In control cells, we observed a dense meshwork of thin filaments of medial-apical actin. Knocking down anillin reduced the intensity of this network, while overexpressing anillin drastically reorganized this network into thick bundles of F-actin that could span the entire surface of the cells (Figure 2A,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,E.

claim: Overexpressing anillin drastically reorganized the medial-apical F-actin network into thick bundles of F-actin that could span the entire surface of the cells.
source: In control cells, we observed a dense meshwork of thin filaments of medial-apical actin. Knocking down anillin reduced the intensity of this network, while overexpressing anillin drastically reorganized this network into thick bundles of F-actin that could span the entire surface of the cells (Figure 2A,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,E.

claim: In live cells overexpressing anillin, Anillin-3xmCherry colocalized with the F-actin bundles.
source: In live cells overexpressing anillin, we also observed thick medial-apical bundles of F-actin using a probe for F-actin (Lifeact-GFP), and Anillin-3xmCherry colocalized with the F-actin bundles (Figure 2B and Video 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Video 3.

claim: Knocking down anillin resulted in almost a complete loss of myosin II from the apical surface of epithelial cells.
source: In controls, myosin II accumulated on the medial-apical surface in patches that resemble previously described cortical waves of F-actin (Bement et al., 2015) (Figure 2C). Knocking down anillin resulted in almost a complete loss of myosin II from the apical surface of epithelial cells, and when anillin was overexpressed, myosin II was increased and decorated the large bundles of F-actin that formed (Figure 2C,D,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D,F.

claim: When anillin was overexpressed, myosin II was increased and decorated the large bundles of F-actin that formed.
source: In controls, myosin II accumulated on the medial-apical surface in patches that resemble previously described cortical waves of F-actin (Bement et al., 2015) (Figure 2C). Knocking down anillin resulted in almost a complete loss of myosin II from the apical surface of epithelial cells, and when anillin was overexpressed, myosin II was increased and decorated the large bundles of F-actin that formed (Figure 2C,D,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D,F.

claim: Junctions associated with medial-apical F-actin bundles connected perpendicularly to the junction exhibited increased recruitment of vinculin compared to junctions associated with medial-apical bundles that run parallel to the junction.
source: Using junctional vinculin intensity as a readout of contractile forces exerted on junctions (Higashi et al., 2016; Hara et al., 2016), we found that junctions associated with medial-apical F-actin bundles connected perpendicularly to the junction exhibited increased recruitment of vinculin compared to junctions associated with medial-apical bundles that run parallel to the junction (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B and citations to Higashi et al., 2016; Hara et al., 2016.

claim: After laser ablation of medial-apical actin, control cells opened 3.0 ± 0.2 µm perpendicular to the cut site after 18 s.
source: After laser ablation of medial-apical actin (Lifeact-RFP), control cells opened 3.0 ± 0.2 µm perpendicular to the cut site after 18 s. Anillin overexpressing cells recoiled significantly more (5.1 ± 0.4 µm), indicating that the medial-apical actin in these cells stores more tensile force, whereas anillin knockdown cells recoiled less than controls (2.0 ± 0.2 µm) in the perpendicular direction (Figure 3C,D, and Video 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C,D, and Video 4.

claim: Anillin overexpressing cells recoiled significantly more (5.1 ± 0.4 µm) after medial-apical laser ablation, indicating that the medial-apical actin in these cells stores more tensile force.
source: After laser ablation of medial-apical actin (Lifeact-RFP), control cells opened 3.0 ± 0.2 µm perpendicular to the cut site after 18 s. Anillin overexpressing cells recoiled significantly more (5.1 ± 0.4 µm), indicating that the medial-apical actin in these cells stores more tensile force, whereas anillin knockdown cells recoiled less than controls (2.0 ± 0.2 µm) in the perpendicular direction (Figure 3C,D, and Video 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C,D, and Video 4.

claim: Anillin knockdown cells recoiled less than controls (2.0 ± 0.2 µm) in the perpendicular direction after medial-apical laser ablation.
source: After laser ablation of medial-apical actin (Lifeact-RFP), control cells opened 3.0 ± 0.2 µm perpendicular to the cut site after 18 s. Anillin overexpressing cells recoiled significantly more (5.1 ± 0.4 µm), indicating that the medial-apical actin in these cells stores more tensile force, whereas anillin knockdown cells recoiled less than controls (2.0 ± 0.2 µm) in the perpendicular direction (Figure 3C,D, and Video 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C,D, and Video 4.

claim: When apical expansion parallel to the cut site was measured, control, anillin knockdown, and anillin overexpressing cells all opened similar distances after laser ablation of medial-apical F-actin.
source: When apical expansion parallel to the cut site was measured, control, anillin knockdown, and anillin overexpressing cells all opened similar distances after laser ablation of medial-apical F-actin (Figure 3C,E, and Video 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C,E, and Video 4.

claim: After medial-apical ablation, anillin knockdown cells exhibited less local expansion strain compared to controls.
source: We found that after medial-apical ablation, anillin knockdown cells exhibited less local expansion strain compared to controls, while anillin overexpressing cells exhibited more local expansion strain compared to controls (Figure 3F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: After medial-apical ablation, anillin overexpressing cells exhibited more local expansion strain compared to controls.
source: We found that after medial-apical ablation, anillin knockdown cells exhibited less local expansion strain compared to controls, while anillin overexpressing cells exhibited more local expansion strain compared to controls (Figure 3F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Following medial-apical ablation, there was no significant difference in tissue contraction strain between controls and anillin overexpression.
source: Following medial-apical ablation, there was no significant difference in tissue contraction strain between controls and anillin overexpression; however, when anillin was knocked down, the surrounding tissue exhibited less contraction strain compared to controls (Figure 3F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, the surrounding tissue exhibited less contraction strain compared to controls following medial-apical ablation.
source: Following medial-apical ablation, there was no significant difference in tissue contraction strain between controls and anillin overexpression; however, when anillin was knocked down, the surrounding tissue exhibited less contraction strain compared to controls (Figure 3F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Extracellular ATP leads to whole-embryo contraction driven by constriction of the apical surface of cells.
source: We added extracellular ATP, which leads to whole-embryo contraction driven by constriction of the apical surface of cells (Joshi et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014; Higashi et al., 2016) (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Joshi et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014; Higashi et al., 2016.

claim: When ATP was added to one side of the animal hemisphere, control embryos contracted towards the site of ATP addition.
source: When ATP was added to one side of the animal hemisphere, control embryos contracted towards the site of ATP addition (Figure 4A,B and Video 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B and Video 5.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, the contractile response to ATP was attenuated.
source: When anillin was knocked down, the contractile response was attenuated, and when anillin was overexpressed, the contractile response lasted longer (Figure 4B,C, and Video 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B,C, and Video 5.

claim: When anillin was overexpressed, the contractile response to ATP lasted longer.
source: When anillin was knocked down, the contractile response was attenuated, and when anillin was overexpressed, the contractile response lasted longer (Figure 4B,C, and Video 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B,C, and Video 5.

claim: Addition of ATP to control embryos resulted in a large burst of F-actin across the medial-apical surface that dissipated over time.
source: At the cellular level, addition of ATP to control embryos resulted in a large burst of F-actin across the medial-apical surface that dissipated over time (Figure 4D and Video 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Video 6.

claim: The burst of F-actin after ATP addition initially accumulated near the junctions then spread toward the center of the cell.
source: The burst of F-actin initially accumulated near the junctions then spread toward the center of the cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, and Video 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, and Video 6.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, F-actin accumulated transiently and locally at junctions after ATP addition.
source: When anillin was knocked down, F-actin accumulated transient and locally at junctions, which we have previously reported as flares of active RhoA associated with local actin accumulation (Reyes et al., 2014; Stephenson et al., 2019). However, these local actin accumulations did not propagate onto the medial-apical surface and resulted in local junction contraction, but not whole-cell or whole-embryo contraction (Figure 4D–F and Video 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F and Video 6 and citations to Reyes et al., 2014; Stephenson et al., 2019.

claim: When anillin was knocked down, local actin accumulations after ATP addition did not propagate onto the medial-apical surface and resulted in local junction contraction, but not whole-cell or whole-embryo contraction.
source: When anillin was knocked down, F-actin accumulated transient and locally at junctions, which we have previously reported as flares of active RhoA associated with local actin accumulation (Reyes et al., 2014; Stephenson et al., 2019). However, these local actin accumulations did not propagate onto the medial-apical surface and resulted in local junction contraction, but not whole-cell or whole-embryo contraction (Figure 4D–F and Video 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F and Video 6.

claim: When anillin was overexpressed, a burst of medial-apical F-actin similar to controls was observed after ATP addition, and the large bundles of F-actin thickened and became more dynamic.
source: When anillin was overexpressed, a burst of medial-apical F-actin similar to controls was observed, and the large bundles of F-actin thickened and became more dynamic (Figure 4D–F and Video 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F and Video 6.

claim: Knocking down anillin significantly reduced the amount of F-actin accumulation after ATP addition compared to controls.
source: When comparing the change in medial-apical F-actin before and after ATP (baseline and peak), knocking down anillin significantly reduced the amount of F-actin accumulation compared to controls, while overexpressing anillin resulted in no significant change in the amount of F-actin accumulation (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Overexpressing anillin resulted in no significant change in the amount of F-actin accumulation after ATP addition.
source: When comparing the change in medial-apical F-actin before and after ATP (baseline and peak), knocking down anillin significantly reduced the amount of F-actin accumulation compared to controls, while overexpressing anillin resulted in no significant change in the amount of F-actin accumulation (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: In cells induced to apically constrict by Shroom3 overexpression, anillin accumulated across the apical surface of the cell, first near junctions then emanating towards the center of the cell.
source: In cells induced to apically constrict by Shroom3 overexpression, anillin accumulated across the apical surface of the cell, first near junctions then emanating towards the center of the cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpressed Δmyo localized to the medial-apical surface and reorganized F-actin into long bundles that spanned the apical surface similar to Anillin FL.
source: When overexpressed, full length anillin (Anillin FL) localized to the medial-apical surface. Overexpressed Δmyo also localized to the medial-apical surface, although less intensely; nonetheless, Δmyo reorganized F-actin into long bundles that spanned the apical surface similar to Anillin FL (Figure 6B–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Overexpressed Δact localized medial-apically to a similar extent as ∆myo, but only reorganized F-actin into short bundles or no bundles at all.
source: In contrast, overexpressed Δact localized medial-apically to a similar extent as ∆myo, but only reorganized F-actin into short bundles or no bundles at all (Figure 6B–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Overexpressed Δmyoact did not efficiently localize medial-apically or reorganize F-actin robustly.
source: Overexpressed Δmyoact did not efficiently localize medial-apically or reorganize F-actin robustly (Figure 6B–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Both the myosin II- and F-actin-binding domains contribute to localization of anillin to the medial-apical surface.
source: These results suggest that both the myosin II- and F-actin-binding domains contribute to localization of anillin to the medial-apical surface, and anillin's F-actin-binding domain is necessary for reorganizing medial-apical F-actin into long bundles
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that deletion of either domain affects localization.

claim: Anillin's F-actin-binding domain is necessary for reorganizing medial-apical F-actin into long bundles.
source: These results suggest that both the myosin II- and F-actin-binding domains contribute to localization of anillin to the medial-apical surface, and anillin's F-actin-binding domain is necessary for reorganizing medial-apical F-actin into long bundles
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that deletion of the F-actin-binding domain prevents long bundle formation.

claim: When overexpressed, both Anillin FL and ΔRBD were able to robustly localize to the medial-apical surface.
source: When overexpressed, both Anillin FL and ΔRBD were able to robustly localize to the medial-apical surface, while medial-apical localization of ΔC2 and ΔPH were reduced (Figure 6F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: Medial-apical localization of ΔC2 and ΔPH were reduced when overexpressed.
source: When overexpressed, both Anillin FL and ΔRBD were able to robustly localize to the medial-apical surface, while medial-apical localization of ΔC2 and ΔPH were reduced (Figure 6F,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: Overexpression of ΔRBD, ΔC2, and ΔPH did not result in structuring of medial-apical F-actin into long or short bundles.
source: Overexpression of ΔRBD, ΔC2, and ΔPH did not result in structuring of medial-apical F-actin into long or short bundles, appearing similar to the negative control cells (Figure 6F,H)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F,H.

claim: Anillin's F-actin-binding and Rho-binding domains are necessary for structuring medial-apical F-actin into long bundles that span the apical surface.
source: Together, these results indicate that anillin's F-actin-binding and Rho-binding domains are necessary for structuring medial-apical F-actin into long bundles that span the apical surface, and anillin's medial-apical localization is facilitated by actomyosin binding with possible contributions from binding to the plasma membrane, regulators of RhoA, or Septins
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that deletion of these domains prevents long bundle formation.

claim: Anillin's medial-apical localization is facilitated by actomyosin binding with possible contributions from binding to the plasma membrane, regulators of RhoA, or Septins.
source: Together, these results indicate that anillin's F-actin-binding and Rho-binding domains are necessary for structuring medial-apical F-actin into long bundles that span the apical surface, and anillin's medial-apical localization is facilitated by actomyosin binding with possible contributions from binding to the plasma membrane, regulators of RhoA, or Septins
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that various domains contribute to localization.

claim: Anillin stabilizes F-actin by preventing Cofilin severing of actin filaments.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tian et al., 2015.

claim: After photobleaching in control cells, Actin-mNeon recovered to 77 ± 2%.
source: After photobleaching in control cells, Actin-mNeon recovered to 77 ± 2%, whereas in cells overexpressing anillin, Actin-mNeon recovered to 57 ± 4% (Figure 7A–C), indicating that anillin stabilizes actin filaments
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: In cells overexpressing anillin, Actin-mNeon recovered to 57 ± 4% after photobleaching.
source: After photobleaching in control cells, Actin-mNeon recovered to 77 ± 2%, whereas in cells overexpressing anillin, Actin-mNeon recovered to 57 ± 4% (Figure 7A–C), indicating that anillin stabilizes actin filaments
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: Anillin stabilizes actin filaments.
source: After photobleaching in control cells, Actin-mNeon recovered to 77 ± 2%, whereas in cells overexpressing anillin, Actin-mNeon recovered to 57 ± 4% (Figure 7A–C), indicating that anillin stabilizes actin filaments

claim: Anillin requires its actin-binding domain to stabilize medial-apical F-actin.

claim: After treating embryos with jasplakinolide (20 µM, 1 hr), increased F-actin bundles at the medial-apical surface were observed.

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment strongly reduced parallel recoil after junctional laser ablation, from 2.7 ± 0.3 µm after 18 s in controls to 0.2 ± 0.1 µm after 18 s.
source: Indeed, jasplakinolide treatment strongly reduced parallel recoil, from 2.7 ± 0.3 µm after 18 s in controls to 0.2 ± 0.1 µm after 18 s (Figure 7E,F, and Video 8)

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment of anillin knockdown embryos also reduced junction recoil after laser ablation.

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment did not increase the number of cells that separate perpendicularly compared to controls.

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment rescued perpendicular separation rates in anillin knockdown cells.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: F-actin stability contributes to the mechanical changes observed in epithelial cells when anillin is perturbed.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that anillin stabilizes medial-apical F-actin and suggest that F-actin stability contributes to the mechanical changes observed in epithelial cells when anillin is perturbed
evidence: The claim is inferred from the jasplakinolide experiments showing similar effects to anillin overexpression.

claim: Regions of the dorsal isolates where anillin was knocked down showed a marked reduction in junctional and medial-apical F-actin compared with internal control regions.

claim: Anillin knockdown disrupted cell morphology causing doming in both ectodermal and endodermal cells.

claim: In mesodermal cells, anillin knockdown disrupted the stereotypic patterning, leading to elongated cell size and accumulation of F-actin at cellular poles along the long axis of the cells.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: When anillin knockdown cells were found in the notochord, they exhibited irregular shapes, abnormal F-actin accumulation, disrupted the stereotypic cross-sectional ellipsoid shape of the notochord itself, and disrupted tissue interfaces between notochord, somite and medial endoderm.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the stiffness of dorsal isolates when anillin was knocked down compared with controls.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Anillin promotes tissue stiffness.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that anillin promotes tissue stiffness, which may be due to anillin's role in organizing medial-apical F-actin
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing reduced tissue stiffness when anillin is knocked down.

claim: Anillin is a scaffolding protein with diverse binding capabilities, which it uses to organize the cytoskeletal elements including F-actin, Septins, and microtubules.
source: Anillin is a scaffolding protein with diverse binding capabilities, which it uses to organize the cytoskeletal elements including F-actin, Septins, and microtubules (Field and Alberts, 1995; Sisson et al., 2000; Silverman-Gavrila et al., 2008; D'Avino, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Field and Alberts, 1995; Sisson et al., 2000; Silverman-Gavrila et al., 2008; D'Avino, 2009.

claim: Anillin builds actin structures by activating formins.

claim: Anillin promotes contractility by linking F-actin and myosin II to the plasma membrane and binding active RhoA and its regulators.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Field and Alberts, 1995; Piekny and Maddox, 2010; Amini et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Junctional laser ablation is thought to measure the amount of line tension or tension in the direction parallel to the edge of a cell.

claim: Initially during Drosophila germ band elongation, tissue tension is transmitted primarily through junctional structures, but by the end of germ band elongation, it is carried by cortex-spanning structures.
